Want Ubuntu, Windows 11 or a fresh copy of macOS on your Mac? Open Burrow, click +, pick a system and click Download & Create. Burrow fetches the installer from the publisher, checks it, builds the machine and starts setup. That's it. [...] Burrow is a native SwiftUI app built on Apple's Virtualization.framework, plus `burrowctl`, a command-line tool for running the same machines headless in scripts and on servers. Everything runs locally, and the code is MIT licensed.

Note

Burrow is an original implementation. Parallels Desktop was studied only at the architecture level (which components exist and which system frameworks they use); no code was copied or translated.

## Quick start

### Requirements

 Apple silicon Mac (M1 or newer) on macOS 14 Sonoma or later
 Xcode with Swift 6 to build from source
 For Windows 11 guests: QEMU (`brew install qemu`)

### Build and run

```
cd# → build/Burrow.app and build/burrowctl #
``` [...] Linux and macOS guests run directly on Virtualization.framework, booting through UEFI (Linux) or Apple's macOS installer.
 Windows 11 on ARM guests run under QEMU with Hypervisor.framework acceleration, since Windows' boot manager hangs under Virtualization.framework. The screen, keyboard and mouse stay in Burrow's window (VNC over a private socket), on UEFI firmware with an NVMe disk that Windows supports out of the box.
 For Windows, Burrow generates a setup disc with an `autounattend.xml` that skips Setup's TPM and Secure Boot checks and allows a local account without a network. It installs the virtio-win ARM64 drivers (networking and others) at first sign-in. Burrow presses the "boot from CD" key for you, and the installer is only attached while the disk is still empty.

# 6 tools for running Windows & Linux on macOS

Published on August 7, 2024

6 tools for running Windows & Linux on macOS

I’ve been happily using Parallels Desktop for my Windows and Linux virtual machine needs for about the past three years. It’s performant, supports a reasonable variety of guest operating systems, and, with some tweaks, can also run headless developer machines and Kubernetes clusters.

However, times are financially lean, so every time I see that recurring fee approaching, I wonder if there are any alternatives. With VMware making Fusion Pro free for personal use in May, it seemed a good time to survey the desktop emulation landscape. [...] In recent months I bought a mini PC for testing and benchmarking. It primarily runs Linux, but came with Windows, so there’s also a bit of me that wonders if I even need a Windows virtual machine eating up drive space anymore. So, if that requirement is becoming less necessary for me, a free option looks even more attractive.

VMware’s post that Fusion is now free for personal use sparked this thought process. Maybe Broadcomm’s recent acquisition prompted the change, or perhaps the company considers it a “gateway product” to bigger and more lucrative options. The corporate nature of Broadcom and VMware makes it a hellish experience to jump through the umpteen account creation steps to try and download it. Pro tip: if you use Homebrew, you can install it with that and bypass all of them 😌.

That aside, the performance overall was good. Strangely, downloading and installing was slower than with Parallels, and creating additional disk space was complicated. Showing its VMware heritage, it also has features for use with containers and Kubernetes.
